title: TB9-28150
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim. She asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the negative determination of the RPD and either grant her claim for protection or, to refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act ("the Act"),1 the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection and dismisses the appeal.
In XXXX 2007, the appellant travelled to Canada.

In April 2016, the appellant initiated an application for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds ("H&C"). Her H&C application was refused in February 2017. Her second H&C application was denied in January 2019.
In January 2019, the appellant initiated an inland claim for refugee protection alleging a fear of persecution by her former boyfriend "XXXX" in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

The appellant's claim was heard by the RPD on September 11, 2019. By a decision dated September 24, 2019, the RPD rejected the appellant's claim. The determinative issues included credibility and state protection.
The appellant argues the RPD erred, including by making multiple obvious mistakes of fact; applying incorrect evidentiary standards; and, by making unreasonable and unwarranted demands.

The RAD is not persuaded that the RPD erred. The RPD correctly concluded that the appellant failed to credibly establish her claim. The RPD also correctly concluded the appellant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection.
The panel has conducted an independent assessment of the evidence to assess whether the RPD decision is correct.2 Admissibility of New Evidence

The burden of proof for admitting new evidence lies with the appellant and is subject to strict criteria. 3 Subsection 110(4) of the Act provides that the appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of her claim or that was not reasonably available, or that she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection of her claim. The RAD Rules require the appellant "must" explain how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to her.4
Further, if the evidence does meet the statutory requirements, the RAD must also decide if the proposed evidence is new, credible and relevant before it can be accepted.
The appellant has submitted several proposed documents very generally arguing they are "new" because they post-date the RPD's decision. Letters from family and friends

The appellant has submitted five letters from her family and friends in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, specifically from her mother "XXXX XXXX", brother "XXXX XXXX," and three friends "XXXX XXXX", "XXXX XXXX" and "XXXX XXXX XXXX The mother's letter is dated November 19, 2019 while the other four letters are all dated November 27, 2019.

The letters are seemingly "new" since they are dated after the rejection of the appellant's claim in September 2019. However, the RAD notes the appellant already provided letters from these same individuals to the RPD, as well as related submissions. Since that time, the appellant has not returned to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines nor met with these individuals. She has similarly not had any contact with XXXX since 2006-2007. As such, the appellant has failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why the contents of these "new" letters were not provided to the RPD before the rejection of her claim.

Moreover, the proposed "new" letters appear to have to been drafted in response to the RPD's findings. For example, the new letters attempt to address the apparent shortcomings in the previously submitted letters, as well as the issues of continuing risk and state protection. The RAD further notes the letters were not sworn to nor witnessed, and none of the purported authors were presented as potential witnesses to the RAD to provide sworn testimony and/or to be cross-examined about the source and circumstances of the creation of the documents, as well as about the accuracy and authenticity of their contents. As such, the RAD finds the proposed letters to have little probative value, even if admitted.

Accordingly, the RAD finds the appellant has failed to meet her burden for admitting the letters as new evidence. In particular, she failed to demonstrate the documents are "new" within the statutory requirements. As was specified by the Federal Court of Appeal, "the role of the RAD is not to provide the opportunity to complete a deficient record submitted before the RPD, but to allow for errors of fact, errors in law or mixed errors of fact and law to be corrected".5 In this regard, the Court has also been very clear that the role of the RAD is not to provide a "second chance" to present a claim. Psychotherapist report by XXXX XXXX

The appellant submitted a psychotherapist report by XXXX XXXX, dated 15 November 2019. This report is dated after the rejection of the appellant's claim. However, the appellant has again failed to demonstrate that the report is "new" within the statutory requirements. For example, she has again failed to provide an explanation as to why she could not reasonably have been expected to present such a report to the RPD. There is no indication she sought to provide such a report to the RPD before the rejection of her claim. In this regard, the appellant had ample time to assemble her documents for her claim and was also represented by counsel.

The RAD also notes Ms. XXXX does not recommend the appellant be designated a "vulnerable person" in her proceedings before the RPD nor RAD. The appellant's counsel before the RPD (and RAD) similarly did not request this or, any special accommodations. Ms. XXXX nevertheless makes pronouncements about the appellant's mental health and wellbeing, including "should she be forced to return to St. Vincent and the Grenadines". Her conclusions and clear advocacy - based merely upon one meeting "typically extending for 60-90 minutes" - bring her objectivity into question. Further, the bulk of the information in Ms. XXXX report is a summary of allegations and symptoms self-reported by the appellant. As the court stated in Danailov, "opinion evidence is only as valid as the truth of the facts on which it is based."6 Further, reports such as this one cannot possibly serve "as a cure-all for deficiencies in the Applicant's evidence" in an RPD (or RAD) decision.7 Finally, the RAD notes Ms. XXXX is not a medical doctor nor qualified to make medical diagnosis.

The RAD accordingly finds the appellant has failed to meet her burden for admitting the report as new evidence. Specifically, she failed to demonstrate it is "new" within the statutory requirements, as well as relevant for the purposes of this appeal. Copy of passport

The appellant also submitted a copy of a page from her passport issued in 2005. The appellant has again not provided a reasonable explanation why she did not provide this document to the RPD before the rejection of her claim. The appellant was represented by counsel and there is no indication she sought to provide it to the RPD before the rejection of her claim. As such, she has failed to meet her burden of proof for admitting the document.

Accordingly, having carefully reviewed all the proposed documents and the appellant's accompanying submissions, the RAD finds the appellant has failed to meet her burden for admitting the "new evidence" in compliance with the statutory requirements. Specifically, the appellant failed to establish that the evidence arose after the RPD decision; was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; and, that she could not have reasonably been expected in the circumstances to have brought this information to the RPD before the decision. In Singh at para 638, the Federal Court of Appeal emphasized that the RAD cannot disregard the clear statutory criteria.9The proposed documents are therefore not admitted as new evidence. Request for an Oral Hearing
No new evidence has been accepted. Accordingly, an oral hearing has not been held. The RPD's Findings
The onus is on the refugee claimant/appellant to establish her claim for protection. The RPD found the appellant had not met her burden to do so. Credibility

The RPD also had a number of credibility concerns with the appellant and her allegations of persecution. For example, the RPD took a negative inference due to omissions in her Basis of Claim (BOC) form regarding any continuing risk from XXXX.
The appellant argues the RPD erred because it did not follow the Maldonado presumption of truth and failed to engage with her explanations.

The RAD disagrees with the appellant's arguments. The RPD provided clear and intelligible reasons as to why the appellant failed to establish the allegations underlying her refugee claim. In this regard, the RPD's credibility concerns were also put to the appellant during the hearing, including about the omissions in her own evidence and whether the appellant faced any continuing risk from XXXX. The RPD did not find the appellant's responses to be reasonable under the circumstances. The RAD agrees. For example, the RAD notes the appellant was represented by counsel and had ample time to amend her narrative, particularly with the central elements of her claim i.e., whether she faced any continuing threats from XXXX. This is not a minor issue, as XXXX is the only agent of persecution.

The RAD also finds the lack of objective evidence, such as hospital records or police reports, to be a relevant and valid factor for the RPD to have considered in assessing the credibility of the allegations. Accordingly, the RAD sees no reason to interfere with the RPD's credibility findings because they are correct and based upon the evidence in the record. Delay in Claiming

The appellant travelled to Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2007. She did not make her claim for refugee protection until January 23, 2019. The RPD therefore took a negative inference as to the appellant's subjective fear and overall credibility due to her delay in seeking refugee protection.

The appellant argues the RPD erred, including because the RPD incorrectly calculated the delay as being fourteen years long. She also submits she was not vulnerable to removal until her second H&C application was denied in 2019. She also argues she provided a plausible explanation for her delay because she had no knowledge about immigration and refugee law.

Having independently reviewed the evidence, the RAD disagrees with the appellant's arguments. The RAD notes the appellant is well-travelled, educated (both in her country and in Canada), and fluent in English. She also has work experience (both in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and Canada) and has been independently supporting herself while in Canada. She is therefore not unsophisticated. Moreover, she was represented by immigration counsel since at least 2016. Yet, she did not initiate her claim for protection until 2019. By her own admission, she was out-of-status since October 2007. As such, the total period of delay - whether twelve or fourteen years - is considerable. While not determinative on its own, the RAD accordingly finds the appellant's failure to seek protection earlier, and her corresponding reason for not doing so, undermines her subjective fear, as well as the credibility of her allegations.

The Court has confirmed that the Board is entitled to consider a refugee claimant's delay in bringing forth a claim, and while delays need not be determinative, they can fatally impugn an applicant's credibility such that the claim is rejected (Hartono v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 601 at para 21 and Espinosa v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2003 FC 1324 at para 17). Documents
The RPD gave little weight to the appellant's supporting letters due to credibility concerns and noting they were primarily based upon hearsay.
The appellant argues the RPD erred by failing to engage in her explanations for any apparent problems with her documents.

The RAD disagrees with the appellant's argument. The RPD demonstrated that it considered the documentary evidence, as well as putting any apparent problems with the evidence to the appellant i.e., noting very obvious concerns clear on the face of the documents, such as the letters all being very similar in nature and having the same format, exact same punctuation mistakes, lack of identity documents attached to them, and the use of the same contact, a P.O. Box. The RAD agrees with the RPD's conclusion that the appellant failed to provide a reasonable explanation to address these credibility concerns. The Court has also been clear that the RPD is entitled to give little weight to documents that corroborate an allegation it finds not to be credible without necessarily making an explicit finding as to their authenticity.10 The Court in Gebetas confirms, "as stated by this Court numerous times, general findings of lack of credibility can affect all relevant evidence submitted by an applicant, including documentary evidence, and ultimately cause the rejection of a claim."11

Accordingly, the panel finds the RPD's analysis and the minimal weight given to the appellant's documents are in accordance with settled law; including that when a general negative credibility finding is made, it is open for the RPD to give low probative value to other documents. As stated by the courts: [c]onsequently, in my opinion, the applicant's assertion that the Board is bound to analyze the documentary evidence "independently from the applicant's testimony" must be examined in the context of the informal proceedings which prevail before the Board. Once a Board, as the present Board did, comes to the conclusion that an applicant is not credible, in most cases, it will necessarily follow that the Board will not give that applicant's documents much probative value, unless the applicant has been able to prove satisfactorily that the documents in question are truly genuine. In the present case, the Board was not satisfied with the applicant's proof and refused to give the documents at issue any probative value. Put another way, where the Board is of the view, like here, that the applicant is not credible, it will not be sufficient for the applicant to file a document and affirm that it is genuine and that the information contained therein is true. Some form of corroboration or independent proof will be required to "offset" the Board's negative conclusion on credibility.12
The RAD accordingly sees no reason to interfere with the RPD's finding giving little weight to the appellant's documents because it is correct and based upon the evidence. State Protection
The RPD also determined the appellant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection.
The appellant argues the RPD erred, including by unduly discounting or ignoring the country documents.

The RAD disagrees with the appellant's argument. The RPD is presumed to have considered the evidence before it, including the appellant's testimony and the country conditions documents. There is no evidence to the contrary. Having also independently reviewed the evidence, the RAD notes Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is a parliamentary democracy. The country documents indicate state protection mechanisms are available for victims of domestic violence - albeit not perfect. As such, the appellant has not met her "heavy burden" to show why she should not have been required to exhaust the state protection recourses available to her domestically. In this regard, the appellant failed to provide any objective evidence to corroborate any efforts to seek state protection. Further, she has been out of the country since 2007.

The RAD has also independently considered the appellant's circumstances. For example, she is now thirty-five years old. She is fluent in English, has completed high school, as well as having attended post-secondary education in Canada. She has been gainfully employed and independently supporting herself for several years. Further, she has several supportive family members and friends in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Finally, she has had no contact with XXXX since approximately 2006 or 2007, which is approximately fourteen years ago.

Finally, the RPD (nor RAD) is not obliged to prove that Saint Vincent and the Grenadines can offer the appellant effective state protection, rather, the appellant bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that adequate state protection exists with "clear and convincing" evidence. The appellant has not met her burden to do so.

Accordingly, having independently considered the evidence and the applicable jurisprudence, the RAD finds that neither the objective evidence nor the appellant's evidence rebuts the presumption of state protection. The RAD therefore finds the appellant has failed to meet her burden to rebut the presumption of state protection. The issue of state protection is determinative of the appellant's claim.

Based on the findings noted above, and in accordance with the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines,13 the RAD finds that the RPD's refugee determination is correct. The appellant simply failed to provide sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to establish her claim, including that she faced any continuing risk from XXXX. The appellant also failed to rebut the presumption of state protection. This is also determinative of the claim.
Contrary to her submissions to the RAD, she also failed to establish falling within the compelling reasons exception.

Accordingly, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection and dismisses the appeal. (signed) "D. Goff " D.
